extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of Restoration drama; playwrights, critics, and editors interested in Dryden and 17th-century theatre
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical commentary on what makes a Restoration-era play succeed or fail — covering plot action, originality, tone, satire, theatrical devices, audience reception, and issues of borrowing/plagiarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality as mode_of_treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: “originality consists in the mode of treating a subject, more than in the subject itself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume a subject is original merely because it is new; the poet's distinctive handling, perspective, structure, or dramatic treatment is what constitutes originality. Even when drawing from existing romances or translations, the author must transform the material by manner, emphasis, or dramatic technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid a 'lame' action (vigor of plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author in the dedication explicitly hints at the 'lameness of the action' as a cause for a play's failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the dramatic action is lively, coherent, and credible; a weak or listless central action will lose audience engagement. Plot must move with purpose and avoid long stretches that feel inert or tangential to the main conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity of titles and topical associations
rubrics_metrics.description: The play's 'second title of "Love in a Nunnery"' may have provoked suspicions of ridicule toward public figures or religion and contributed to its poor reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful that titles or subtitles can invite political, religious, or social readings; avoid phrasing that might suggest an attack on powerful institutions or provoke misinterpretation unless such provocation is intentional and accounted for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inelegant or vulgar theatrical devices
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'absurd and vulgar scene, in which the prince pretends a fit of the cholic,' is singled out as likely contributing to the play's failure; called an 'inelegant jeu de theatre.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from including buffoonish or grotesque set-pieces that interrupt tone or taste. Theatrical tricks or farcical stunts should serve character or theme; gratuitous stage effects risk alienating audiences and critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach by example rather than dull didacticism
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Not with dull morals, gravely writ... but by examples drawn, I dare to say, From most of you who hear and see the play.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral or instructive aims are more effective when dramatized through concrete examples and relatable situations rather than sermonizing. Show behavior and consequences onstage rather than delivering abstract moralizing speeches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation and self-awareness in satire
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘He would not quite the women's frailty bare, But stript them to the waist, and left them there: And the men's faults are less severely shown, For he considers that himself is one.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire should be measured and self-aware; over-exposure or one-sided, merciless ridicule can seem crude or hypocritical. The author should temper attacks and recognize shared human faults to avoid alienating the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use representative samples rather than exhaustive vilification
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘He spared my shame... He spared my shame, which you, I'm sure, would not, For you were all for driving on the plot: You sighed when I came in to break the sport, And set your teeth when each design fell short. To wives and servants all good wishes lend, But the poor cuckold seldom finds a friend.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is often sufficient to present specimens or samples of social 'stuff' (vices, follies) rather than attempting to catalogue or vilify every instance. Selective portrayal can be more effective and less tiresome than exhaustive denunciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience taste and fickleness matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The text observes that an audience may capriciously condemn a play 'not worse than many others which they received with applause' and that 'bad taste and unjust preferences of the age' affected reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that success depends partly on contemporary audience tastes and fashions; even competent plays may fail if they clash with prevailing preferences. Authors should consider the audience's sensibilities but also weigh whether to conform or challenge them intentionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid blatant borrowing without transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Critiques of translators and adaptors (Ravenscroft, Langbaine) emphasize borrowing: 'he borrowed from romance, and did translate' and the repeated discussion of plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If adapting or translating existing material, the author must contribute clear creative value (new treatment, perspective, or form). Mere patchwork translation or slavish copying invites censure as plagiarism; transform source material rather than reproducing it.
